intro: Five long reads for a slow week: who should set the speed of AI, what a wealth tax does to a company's soul, why cheap weapons shrink empires, what it would mean for space to be a projection, and a close reading of Romans 1 on why we resist what we already know.

stories.headline: A thousand strangers to set the speed limit
stories.dek: Hélène Landemore and Audrey Tang propose a standing global citizens' assembly to decide how fast frontier AI should move, and to hold labs to their word.
body: In the middle of September, the people running the world's leading AI labs said something unusual in public. By Hélène Landemore and Audrey Tang's account, Anthropic's Dario Amodei called for easing the pace of frontier development and offered independent evaluators ongoing, employee-like access to his company's systems. OpenAI's Sam Altman agreed that the frontier needed pacing and made the same pledge. Elon Musk added his assent. None of it came with a timetable, a shared standard or anyone to check.

Landemore, a political theorist at Yale, and Tang, Taiwan's former digital minister and now its cyber ambassador, take those statements at face value and ask the obvious next question. If the builders want to slow down, why can't they? Their essay in Noema is an answer to that question and a proposal for fixing it.
## A stag hunt, not a prisoner's dilemma

The authors describe a double collective-action problem. Inside America, labs race each other. Between America and China, governments race too, and 'if we slow down, China wins' is the standard argument against binding rules at home. Each race excuses the other.

The tempting model is the prisoner's dilemma, in which defection always pays and cooperation needs coercion. Landemore and Tang reach instead for Rousseau's stag hunt. A party of hunters can catch a stag only if everyone holds position; any one of them can break ranks and catch a hare. The stag is better for all. What makes people chase hares is not preference but doubt that the others will hold. In the authors' reading, nobody at the frontier actually prefers the hare. The binding constraint is trust.

That distinction matters because the cure is different. A stag hunt is solved not by force but by assurance: credible, visible evidence that others are keeping their side of the bargain. And here the current arrangements fail. Evaluators hired by the labs, judging against risk thresholds the labs define, cannot reassure a rival lab, let alone a rival government. Evidence changes behaviour only when it flows to a party that none of the competitors controls.
## Who could be the witness?

The obvious candidate is the United Nations. The authors dismiss it quickly. The Security Council gives both Washington and Beijing a veto, and the UN is an assembly of sovereigns; it cannot stand above the very states whose race is the problem. Their alternative is more radical. The only party whose stake is universal and whose partiality is not national or corporate, they argue, is humanity itself.
## The design

The proposal is a Global Citizens' Assembly on AI: 1,000 people drawn by lottery from every continent, sitting continuously rather than producing a single report and disbanding. The lottery is meant to reach people who never appear in policy debates, including the young, the rural, the illiterate and the unconnected. Seats would follow population, which gives China roughly one in six.

Members would serve fixed part-time terms, with a third of the seats redrawn regularly so the body keeps its memory without hardening into a new elite. Deliberation would happen online with local support, over months, with professional facilitation, interpretation, secure communications and pay for participants. AI tools would translate and sort contributions, but members could overrule any machine summary.

Two features do the real work. First, the independent evaluators who audit the labs would be vetted under rules the assembly sets, reversing today's arrangement in which labs pick their own monitors. Second, every recommendation would name the institutions it addresses and set a deadline by which each must answer in public: what it accepts, what it rejects, and why.

The size is deliberate. A body as large as a parliament is not a focus group. A chief executive can shrug off a critic; refusing to answer a thousand people drawn from every continent means refusing in public, with reasons, on a planetary stage.
## Teeth, precedent and legitimacy

For enforcement the authors look to Brussels. Since August 2026 the EU's AI Office has had power to fine frontier-model providers or order mitigations and recalls, and the major labs have signed the safety chapters of its code of practice. Those codes treat the public as an input. Amending them so that signatories must answer the assembly would turn a moral duty into a legal one, at least inside the EU.

On feasibility they point to a long record. The OECD counts more than 800 deliberative bodies worldwide. A 100-member Global Assembly deliberated alongside COP26. Meta ran a Community Forum with 6,300 people across 32 countries. Anthropic convened about a thousand Americans to help draft model principles in 2023, and Taiwan brought 447 citizens together online on AI integrity in 2024.

They are careful not to claim that lottery confers legitimacy automatically. The assembly would have to earn moral authority by the quality of its procedures, and that authority would harden into political legitimacy only as lawful institutions chose to recognise duties toward it.
## Objections, answered in passing

Beijing has repeatedly denounced 'exclusive groups' in AI governance. The authors turn that against it: a population-weighted lottery is the least Western-dominated forum available. If China stays out, its absence is visible; if it joins and opens its labs to vetted evaluators, both key hunters are in the same room.

On competence, members would commission competing expertise and allow outside challenges to findings. On capture, an independent civic secretariat would pool disclosed funding and keep funders away from recruitment and evidence. On speed, the authors accept a tension: urgency is real, but it cannot justify skipping the deliberation that makes the frontier answerable to anyone.

Their concrete asks come in three steps: a coalition of governments and foundations funds the secretariat; labs widen their evaluator pledges so assembly-vetted evaluators report to the assembly and labs accept a duty to respond; and labs pilot transparent safety-research budgets of 5–20% of compute under published accounting. Start now, they say, and a first cohort could sit by spring 2027. If the catastrophe never comes, the world will still have built a tool for other planetary problems, from climate to migration.
stories.counterpoint: Legitimacy is not leverage. Outside the EU, a lab can publicly decline a recommendation at little cost, and the stag hunt is broken by verification and enforcement rather than by the moral weight of the witness. The essay is strongest on diagnosis and thinnest on how the assembly would detect and punish a lab or state that quietly keeps racing. It also leans on the good faith of CEO statements that were, by the authors' own account, vague.
stories.why: Most AI-governance proposals assume a regulator or a treaty can impose restraint. This one treats coordination under mistrust as the core problem and designs for assurance, which is the right diagnosis. The cheap test is whether any lab accepts the duty to answer an outside body in public by a deadline. If none does, the pledges to slow down were hares all along.

source.title: Let The People Set The Pace Of Frontier AI
source.author: Hélène Landemore & Audrey Tang

questions: If you ran a frontier lab, what would make you believe a rival was really slowing down: a pledge, an audit, or a witness neither of you controls?
Does random selection give an assembly more legitimacy than expertise, or only a different kind?
What would count as success for this assembly in its first two years, short of stopping the race?

stories.headline: What a wealth tax takes that money cannot measure
stories.dek: Palladium argues that taxing founders on paper valuations forces them to sell the one thing a private company exists to protect: control.
body: In November Californians will vote on Proposition 40, a one-time tax of up to 5% on the wealth of billionaire residents. The arguments on both sides are familiar. Supporters say the state's technology booms made a few people extraordinarily rich while public services strained, and that those people should give some back. Opponents say billionaires and their companies will leave, taking tax revenue with them.

Christian Angelopoulos's long essay in Palladium sets both arguments aside. Each, he says, assumes that what is being taxed is just money. His claim is that for a founder or a family owner, much of what a valuation measures is not money at all but the power to run an institution for a purpose of one's own choosing, and that a wealth tax converts that power into a cash liability that can only be paid by giving the power away.
## The clause that targets control

The mechanism sits in the drafting. Proposition 40 says that where an interest carries voting or other control rights, the taxpayer's ownership share is presumed to be no less than their share of those control rights. In plain terms, voting power is valued as a slice of the company's market capitalisation. Ordinary appraisal practice treats control differently from economic ownership; this rule fuses them, and in doing so makes control itself the thing being assessed.
## In-N-Out

His running example is In-N-Out Burger. Lynsi Snyder, granddaughter of the founders, owns the chain outright; in 75 years it has never sold shares or taken outside capital. That is why it can refuse to franchise, keep a tiny menu, pay managers six-figure salaries and print Bible references on its cups. Snyder has said the business is not about the money and that she would sell only if God changed her heart by a lightning bolt.

She announced a move to Tennessee in July, citing the difficulty of raising a family in California; Proposition 40 was filed three months later. Had she stayed, Angelopoulos argues, the tax would have forced her to sell shares, and the first outside shareholder would change the company's legal character even before she lost a majority.
## Alice and Acme

To show why, he builds a worked example. Alice founded Acme Corp five years ago and, after several funding rounds, still owns just over half. In the latest round outside investors bought 1% of the company in preferred shares at a $10 billion valuation. Headlines would say Alice is worth $5 billion.

That number, he argues, is an inference from one small trade in a different security. Alice holds common stock in a private company, with transfer restrictions and no market price. Assessed at $5 billion, she owes $250 million she does not have. To raise it she must sell a block of private stock: hire bankers, find buyers able to spend hundreds of millions, work through rights of first refusal and board consent, perhaps offer board seats, perhaps seek regulatory approval, all while every counterparty knows she is a forced seller.

Crucially, the price of a 1% sliver does not predict the price of a large block. She will have to sell more shares than the headline arithmetic implies, and that can take her below 50%. At that point she has lost something the tax never priced: the authority to elect the board, appoint managers, allocate capital and decide what the company is for. Acme under Alice and Acme without her may not even be the same asset. The state, as he puts it in effect, has valued her authority and then used that valuation to make her surrender it.
## What one outside shareholder changes

Why does losing sole control matter so much? His legal anchor is eBay v. Newmark, a Delaware case. Craigslist's founders, Craig Newmark and Jim Buckmaster, held more than 70% of the company when eBay bought a minority stake. eBay wanted to monetise the site; the founders saw it as a largely free community service. When eBay launched a competitor, they adopted a rights plan to protect Craigslist's culture. The Court of Chancery struck it down. A for-profit corporation, it held, is not a vehicle for purely philanthropic ends when other stockholders expect a return; directors who chose that form are bound by fiduciary duties to promote value for stockholders.

The lesson Angelopoulos draws is that sole ownership encodes a governance structure in which one person can make choices that diffuse shareholders never would. Introduce outsiders and the founder's mission becomes legally subordinate to their interests. A wealth tax, applied year by year or even once at scale, moves companies from the first world into the second.
## A takings problem?

The essay then turns constitutional. The Fifth Amendment bars taking private property for public use without just compensation. Usually the difference between taxing and taking is obvious. His thought experiment blurs it: in wartime a government needs tungsten under a farmer's land. The discovery triples the land's value. Instead of condemning the land and paying, the state levies a one-off tax of 100% of the new assessed value. The farmer cannot pay without selling, so he sells. Nothing was seized, yet the effect is confiscation without compensation.

At 50%, the same logic holds. At 10%, probably. At 5%, it is gentler but not different in kind. He concedes there is no clean line, and that almost any tax can force some asset sale. His narrower point is that courts already protect intangible business interests and going-concern value, and that a tax which, by its own valuation rule, foreseeably forces founders to surrender control raises the question of whether control is itself protected property.

He notes that the stakes are not only Californian: Representative Ro Khanna has endorsed a federal wealth tax of 2% a year on fortunes above $50 million, a threshold that reaches ordinary founders and family firms.
## Infrastructure of liberty

His closing argument widens the frame. Constitutional rights such as speech and association are legal protections; private companies are how those protections become material capacity. George Lucas could always make any film he liked; owning Lucasfilm let him keep doing it. On this view, forcing independent institutions into diffuse ownership does more than raise revenue. It lets the state convert missions into returns, commodifying precisely the things critics of capitalism usually accuse markets of commodifying.
stories.counterpoint: Designers of wealth taxes know about illiquidity and control: deferral with interest, payment in kind, or allowing non-voting shares to settle the bill are standard fixes, and the essay does not engage them. It also treats concentrated control as a public good, when it equally shields poor governance and entrenched owners from accountability. And the takings argument asks courts to draw a line the author admits does not exist.
stories.why: Wealth-tax debates usually run on revenue and fairness. This piece reframes them around institutional diversity: whether an economy keeps room for firms run by conviction rather than by the median shareholder. That lens travels far beyond California, including to founder-led and family-controlled businesses across Asia, and it is the strongest version of the case you will need to answer if you support such taxes.

source.title: Wealth Taxes Could Kill Privately-Owned Companies
source.author: Christian Angelopoulos

questions: Is the power to run a firm for a non-financial mission a public good worth protecting, or a private privilege the tax code should ignore?
Where would you draw the line between taxing an asset and forcing its sale?
Which institutions you admire exist only because one owner could refuse outside capital?

stories.headline: Iron, drones and the shrinking of empires
stories.dek: Works in Progress argues that when weapons become cheap and local, centralised power loses its grip, as it did at the end of the Bronze Age.
body: In 1274 BC, beside the Orontes river in Syria, the armies of Egypt and the Hittite empire met at Kadesh. Tens of thousands of soldiers and more than 5,000 chariots took part, a battle bigger than Hastings, Agincourt or Yorktown and comparable to some engagements of the first world war. Ramesses II had it carved on temple walls as a triumph, and those reliefs give historians their first detailed reconstruction of a major battle.

The world of Kadesh was a world of great powers: Hittites in Anatolia, Egypt from Sudan to the Levant, Assyria and Babylon contesting Mesopotamia, Mycenaean palaces at Mycenae, Pylos and Thebes. These were bureaucratic states that could tax, conscript and build. Within a few centuries all of them had vanished or shrunk to irrelevance.

Patrick Fitzsimmons's essay in Works in Progress starts from a sharper version of the usual puzzle. Droughts, famines, revolts and the raids of the Sea Peoples around 1200 BC can explain a collapse. Catastrophes happen and states usually recover. What they cannot easily explain is why nothing on the old scale re-emerged for centuries.
## Tin made empires

His answer begins with an ingredient. Bronze is copper alloyed with tin, and tin was rare. The deposits within reach of the Bronze Age world lay in what are now Afghanistan, France, Iberia and Cornwall. Isotope and trace-element studies have found Cornish tin in shipwrecks off Israel and southern France. Texts from Mari, in Syria, show tin arriving in the 18th century BC from Elam, more than 500 miles away, which had itself obtained it perhaps a thousand miles further east. Every leg of that journey carried risk from bandits and hostile states.

Scarcity had a political shape. A large state could secure supply lines, build stockpiles and replace losses; a small one could not. Peripheral communities might resist for a season, but only a palace could keep a competitive army in bronze year after year. The metal itself favoured concentration.
## How iron broke the monopoly

Bronze Age elites knew iron, but mostly as a treasure fallen from the sky; meteoric iron appears among Tutankhamun's grave goods. The obstacle to using terrestrial ore was heat. Tin melts at 232°C and copper at 1,085°C, both within reach of simple furnaces. Iron melts at 1,538°C.

The workaround was the bloomery. Bellows drove extra air into a charcoal furnace to reach about 1,200–1,300°C. That does not melt iron, but it lets carbon monoxide strip oxygen from the ore while impurities run off as slag. What remains is a spongy 'bloom' that smiths hammer to drive out the rest and then reheat and shape. The technique may have originated in India around 1400 BC or in Georgia, probably in more than one place, and spread to Iran, Mesopotamia and the eastern Mediterranean over the following centuries. The western Mediterranean took roughly a millennium.

The striking point is that iron was not a better metal. Good bronze is harder and more predictable, and its lower melting point makes it easy to recycle. Iron won on abundance. It is the fourth most common element in the earth's crust, and its ores announce themselves: black-brown goethite, yellowish limonite, reddish hematite that leaves a rusty streak. Danish Iron Age tools were made from local bog iron smelted with charcoal from nearby woods. A village no longer needed a trade network or a king to arm itself.
## The evidence that violence spread

Ancient writers noticed. Hesiod described the age of iron as one of endless toil and strife. The Hebrew Bible records the Philistines trying to keep smiths away from the Israelites. Lucretius wrote that iron made the odds of war equal as never before.

Fitzsimmons adds numbers. A study of skeletons from the Middle East that distinguishes injuries received in life from post-mortem damage finds more weapon trauma in the Late Bronze and Iron Ages than in the Middle Bronze Age. Databases of battles show a sharp rise in the century after iron arrives compared with the century before, though he notes that some scholars attribute part of this to better records. King lists for Babylon, Assyria and Athens show average reign lengths falling by 29% after iron, and Babylon getting through nearly twice as many kings. He is candid that Athens's early list includes Cecrops, the mythical half-man, half-serpent.
## A map of small powers

No early Iron Age empire approached the scale of its predecessors. Where the Hittites had ruled, a patchwork of small states appeared; the same happened in Greece and the Levant. Out of that fragmented world came the Greek city-states and eventually democracy, Phoenician trade and its alphabet, and the Abrahamic religions. The collapse, on this reading, was less an apocalypse than a redistribution of the means of violence from palace armouries to village forges.

He is careful about causation here. Iron did not arrive and topple empires in a single stroke; the collapse around 1200 BC had several causes. His claim is narrower and in some ways stronger: once cheap iron existed, the old empires could not be rebuilt on the old terms, because the palace had lost its monopoly on the tools that made its armies decisive. The ceiling on central power had moved, and nothing would move it back for a long time.

He sets this inside a longer rhythm. Castles let medieval barons defy kings until gunpowder made walls obsolete and tilted power back to the centre. Then cheap firearms spread power outward again to rebels and irregulars. Nuclear weapons raised the cost of invasion for everyone while letting small nuclear states punch far above their weight.
## Drones, and the AI exception

The modern parallel is the drone. By the figure he cites, drones account for up to 80% of recent casualties in the war in Ukraine as of 2026. A machine costing a few hundred dollars can kill a tank, a gun or a command post worth millions. That lowers the entry price of war and could let small forces, including guerrillas, contest far stronger ones.

His most useful move is to refuse the easy analogy for AI. Widely available models look like iron: capability in everyone's hands. But the frontier is controlled by a few providers who can restrict access to chosen customers. That looks more like tin. Whether a technology decentralises power depends less on how clever it is than on where its scarce input sits and who can gate it.
stories.counterpoint: Single-cause readings of the Bronze Age collapse have a poor track record, and the correlation between iron and instability fits equally well with iron spreading because order had already broken down. Drones may also favour whoever can mass-produce them, which is to say large industrial states. And reign lengths and battle counts from patchy ancient records are fragile evidence to hang a theory of history on.
stories.why: The chokepoint question is a practical tool: for any technology, ask whether its scarce input is local or controlled. It works for drones, for chips and for frontier AI models at once, and it predicts which institutions gain and which lose. For anyone thinking about power over the next decade, that is a sharper lens than asking whether a technology is 'democratising'.
questions: For the technologies shaping your industry, where is the scarce input, and who controls it?
Does cheap, local capability make societies freer, or merely more violent and fragmented, as the Iron Age records suggest?
If frontier AI behaves like tin, what would it take to turn it into iron, and would that be desirable?

stories.headline: If gravity is a hologram, what is real?
stories.dek: Quanta's Charlie Wood asks what three decades of the holographic principle actually say about the world we live in.
body: Charlie Wood has covered holography for Quanta for years. His new essay opens with a confession: for most of that time he did not really understand what it meant. The idea has been called the most profound proposal in theoretical physics of recent decades. It is also, he notes, a strange hybrid: part established mathematics, part speculative leap about reality. His piece is an attempt to separate the two.
## Area, not volume

The story starts with black holes in the 1970s. Entropy is, roughly, a count of how many ways a thing's contents can be arranged, so you would expect it to grow with volume: a bigger box holds more stuff. Jacob Bekenstein and Stephen Hawking found that a black hole's entropy grows instead with the area of its surface.

The physicist Bartek Czech gives Wood an image for how odd that is. It is as if a CT scanner could reconstruct every fold, vessel and neuron of a brain from photographs of its outside. Czech also offers a reason it might be possible for gravity specifically. In electromagnetism, positive and negative charges can cancel, so the field outside a region does not pin down what is inside. Mass comes in only one sign. The way spacetime bends at a boundary therefore carries unusually complete information about what lies within. He calls this a miracle of gravity.
## Susskind's leap

In the 1990s Leonard Susskind, along with Gerard 't Hooft and Charles Thorn working independently, took the entropy result literally: a black hole is a hologram, and its interior adds no information that is not already on the surface. Susskind has said he thought the idea a little crazy but the least crazy of the options.

He then pushed it further. Any region of space can in principle become a black hole if you pack enough mass into it. If black holes are holographic, the argument runs, so is the room you are sitting in.

Not everyone accepts the reasoning. Latham Boyle of the University of Edinburgh argues that two different entropies are being conflated: one counts the particles a region can hold and scales with volume; the other measures quantum entanglement across its boundary and scales with area. On his account nothing mystical follows. He describes his view as more down to earth.
## The snow globe

What turned holography from a suggestive argument into a research programme was the AdS/CFT correspondence of the late 1990s, whose founding papers have gathered tens of thousands of citations. It concerns a peculiar geometry called anti-de Sitter space, curved so that an infinite interior fits inside a finite boundary, like a snow globe. The inside looks like a universe with particles and gravity. The boundary carries a quantum theory of a special kind, a conformal field theory, which looks the same at every scale and contains no gravity at all.

The result is that the two are mathematically the same system described twice. Wood likens it to discovering that every move in checkers can be translated into a legal move in chess. The physicist Sebastian Mizera tells him the analogy undersells it: think checkers into basketball. Unlike the broader holographic principle, Wood stresses, AdS/CFT is essentially a mathematical fact. Brian Swingle's gloss is that gravity and quantum mechanics, long treated as rivals, turn out to be intertwined, with one emerging from the other.
## The problem with our universe

The catch is geometry. Our universe is expanding and resembles de Sitter space, curved the opposite way from the snow globe and with no outer boundary on which to write a hologram. On the face of it, AdS/CFT tells us nothing about the world we inhabit.

Advocates reply with an ant's-eye argument. A creature deep inside a snow globe could not easily tell which way its space curves, so it would be odd if the deep rules differed between the two. Wood reports newer work, including by Susskind, on holographic models of de Sitter space that look very different from AdS/CFT. Rather than compressing a volume onto an area, some compress every dimension into a single quantum point. Vijay Balasubramanian of the University of Pennsylvania thinks even that may not be radical enough: since relativity fused space with time, if space emerges from something spaceless, time should emerge from something timeless too. No such theory yet exists.
## Three answers to 'what is real'
When Wood pressed physicists on what holography implies about reality, most declined. Susskind said capital-T truth was above his pay grade. Balasubramanian offered a map of the options.

The first is that the boundary is real and space is not. This is popular among holographers. On this view we are like characters in a video game, taking pixels on a flat screen for a deep world; the physicist Charles Cao describes us as fooled into thinking there is more stuff than there is. The research programme called 'it from qubit' holds that space emerges from quantum information. Distance becomes a consequence rather than a cause: things do not fail to affect each other because they are far apart; they seem far apart because they do not affect each other, as a game's sun passes behind a tree without burning it.

The second is that the interior is real and the boundary description is a clever mathematical double, useful but not fundamental. Holographers tend to avoid it mainly because they lack a quantum theory of space itself, which Balasubramanian notes is a statement about ignorance, not evidence against it.

The third is that neither is fundamental. Both gravity and the boundary theory would approximate something deeper that no one has written down, as both pixels and game objects rest on electrons moving through a console.

Wood plants his own flag in an extreme form of the first view: reality is made of qubits, but not qubits spread on anything as familiar as a screen. Perhaps they coexist at a single point. He ends more modestly. Physics may never settle what is ultimately real. Its job is to find simple ideas, expressed mathematically, that predict reliably, and holography is one of them: a proven equivalence between area and volume in some spaces, and an open question in ours.
stories.counterpoint: Holography is established in a toy universe with the wrong shape and conjectured in ours. Until there is a working de Sitter version with testable consequences, 'space is emergent' is an interpretation rather than a finding, and Boyle's deflationary reading of black-hole entropy shows the evidential base is less settled than popular accounts suggest.
stories.why: This is the clearest recent guide to one of the ideas shaping how physicists, and increasingly technologists, talk about information, computation and reality. Knowing exactly where the proven mathematics ends and the metaphysics begins is useful well beyond physics, including for anyone engaging claims about emergence, simulation or materialism from a theological standpoint.

source.title: Gravity Seems Holographic. What Does That Mean for Reality?
source.author: Charlie Wood

questions: If space turned out to be emergent from something more basic, what, if anything, would change about how you understand the physical world?
Why do so many physicists decline to say what is 'really real' even when their mathematics is proven?
How would you tell the difference between a deep truth about nature and an elegant mathematical coincidence?

stories.headline: The heart knows, and will not yield
stories.dek: A new exegesis of Romans 1:32 argues that the noetic effects of sin are less a broken intellect than a resisting heart.
body: Romans 1:32 is usually read as a coda, the last line of a long vice list: though they know God's righteous decree that those who practise such things deserve to die, they not only do them but approve of those who practise them. Paul S. Jeon, writing in the summer 2026 issue of Themelios, argues that the verse is not a coda but a key. It tells us what kind of problem unbelief is.

The verse presents a paradox. The people it describes know God's moral will clearly, yet they break it and then celebrate breaking it. Much of the tradition, Jeon says, has explained unbelief chiefly as a failure of the mind. He wants to recover a different reading, in which the root is not ignorance but an emotionally charged refusal of unwelcome truth.
## Reading 1:32 in its setting

Jeon first places the verse inside Romans 1:18–32. The section opens with God's wrath revealed against those who suppress the truth in unrighteousness (1:18), and it is emphatic that the truth is available: what can be known about God is plain to them (1:19); his invisible attributes are clearly perceived in creation (1:20). The starting point is recognition met by refusal, not a blank slate.

What follows is a descent traced in the language of exchange and handing over. People exchange the glory of God for images (1:23) and the truth for a lie (1:25). Three times God gives them over: to impurity (1:24), to dishonourable passions (1:26), to a debased mind (1:28). The pattern, Jeon argues, locates the problem in a refusal to honour God (1:21) that works itself out in progressive deterioration. Verse 32 is where the slope ends: not merely doing evil, but approving it together.
## Four words that carry the argument
The heart of the paper is lexical, drawing on BDAG and on commentators such as Douglas Moo.

Epignontes, the participle translated 'though they know', denotes thorough, experiential knowing rather than vague awareness. It rules out treating these people as uncertain or uninformed; they recognise God's judgment on what they do.
To dikaioma tou theou, 'God's righteous decree', carries judicial weight. It is not an abstract principle but God's authoritative verdict.
Axioi thanatou, 'worthy of death', confirms that the knowledge includes moral accountability: they grasp that the acts deserve divine judgment.

Then comes the contrast between prassontes, those who practise such things, whose present tense suggests settled, sustained conduct, and syneudokousin, those who approve. The second verb, Jeon argues, means more than tolerance. It implies shared delight and active endorsement, even a kind of conspiratorial pleasure in wrongdoing.

Jeon's point about the verbs is that they are cumulative. Knowing is set against doing, and doing against approving, so that each clause tightens the one before. The same people who grasp the verdict go on acting against it, and then gather others around the act. Read this way, the sentence has the shape of an indictment, with knowledge as the aggravating factor rather than the excuse.
## Why approval is worse than doing

That final clause, he says, is the climax. Private transgression violates a standard; public approval of transgression inverts it. It adds a communal dimension in which people draw satisfaction and solidarity from others doing the same, and those networks of mutual validation reinforce and harden the original refusal. Suppression is social as well as individual.
## The tradition on sin and the mind

Jeon then surveys how Reformed theology has handled the noetic effects of sin. Calvin taught that a seed of religion is sown in all, yet the mind is so dulled by sin that it neither receives nor retains the truth, which leaves people culpably ignorant until grace regenerates them. Kuyper widened the point: every faculty, reason included, is shaped by a person's spiritual orientation, so knowledge of God is never neutral. Alvin Plantinga, in his account of warranted Christian belief, argued that belief in God can be properly basic, produced by a sensus divinitatis that sin has damaged or impeded.

Jeon values all three, but he identifies a shared tendency, sharpest in Plantinga: sin's effect is framed mainly as cognitive malfunction, and unbelief as a failure to reason or form beliefs correctly. That, he argues, risks reducing Paul's anthropology to a question of mental capacity and missing the moral and affective character of human resistance.
## The affective model

His alternative comes from N. Gray Sutanto's retrieval of neo-Calvinist sources, especially Herman and Johan Bavinck. Here the sensus divinitatis is not a faculty for inferring propositions but a deep, intuitive awareness of dependence on God. Johan Bavinck spoke of a sensus numinis, a pre-reflective consciousness of the divine that general revelation touches beneath ideas and propositions, in feelings and intuitions.

On this view sin's primary effect is not a distorted mind but a resisting heart. Suppression is a motivated flight from something already perceived. People are unknowing knowers: fugitives from a truth they have, not strangers to it. Johan Bavinck even borrowed the language of repression. Suppression can proceed silently and unconsciously, yet remains real. The knowledge of God is not inaccessible; it is existentially unbearable. It brings anxiety and guilt, and the heart responds with aversion and avoidance.

Jeon names the forces at work as fear, guilt, pride and the desire for autonomy. Acknowledging God means accepting accountability, vulnerability and dependence, which is exactly what sinful affections refuse. Genesis 3, where the man and woman hide among the trees after they sin, is the pattern: shame and fear drive evasion, not confusion.
## For apologetics, pastoral care and preaching

If this is right, the implications are practical. Apologetics becomes less about importing foreign ideas than awakening what has been suppressed and redirecting what has been misdirected. It looks more like compassionate counsel than debate, inviting honest self-examination and drawing out buried guilt and shame. The question shifts from what someone thinks to what they want and what they fear.

Pastoral ministry needs both boldness and tenderness: boldness because the suppressed truth presses on every conscience, tenderness because suppression is often terror at being exposed before holiness. Discipleship must address desires as well as beliefs, and a faithful community becomes a place where suppressed convictions can surface.

Preaching, likewise, must do more than convey propositions. It should name the idols that absorb our worship, such as comfort, autonomy and success, and expose their counterfeit character, always tied to grace. Only grace, Jeon insists, can unmask how deep suppression goes without crushing the one who sees it.
stories.counterpoint: Setting affective against cognitive risks a false dichotomy. Paul says they became futile in their thinking and their foolish hearts were darkened (1:21), and the handing over to a debased mind (1:28) is plainly noetic. Plantinga's model also locates much of the damage in the will's resistance, so the contrast with Reformed epistemology may be sharper in the paper than in the sources.
stories.why: It gives exegetical footing to something every preacher senses: people rarely reject Christ for lack of information. For teaching Romans, or doing apologetics among educated sceptics, it moves the task from winning arguments to naming loves and fears, and it offers a careful word study of 1:32 that could anchor a sermon on why approving sin is its final stage.

questions: Where do you see people resisting the gospel less for intellectual reasons than for what acceptance would cost them?
